title: Canberra Times: Albanese, Chalmers backflip on key budget tax measures
text:

The federal government has executed a series of dramatic policy reversals on its highly contentious budget measures, abandoning sweeping ministerial powers, dumping a tax on deceased estates and expanding capital gains tax concessions for small businesses.

Login or signup to continue reading

It has, in short, had to restructure core revenue-raising measures because of a widespread public backlash. This is a major capitulation for an administration that initially dismissed criticism of the legislation as partisan scaremongering.

The timing raises questions about political strategy and transparency. Only 48 hours before the backflip, Treasurer Jim Chalmers ruled out any imminent carve-outs or exemptions during a media conference. He insisted ongoing consultations with the tech and small business sectors were genuine and incomplete.

Thursday's volte-face suggests that was either a deliberate effort to obfuscate the government's intentions or a swift intervention by a Prime Minister determined to halt a severe slide in political fortunes.

Labor, tellingly, chose to announce the retreat from its unpopular policies in the wake of a controversial speech by Pauline Hanson; a classic deployment of the political tactic known as "taking out the trash".

Under the reworked package, the government lifted the turnover threshold for the 50 per cent small business capital gains tax reduction from $2 million to $10 million. This concession brought an estimated 98 per cent of active businesses into the exemption zone, effectively reversing the Treasurer's earlier insistence that the original boundaries were already adequate.

Furthermore, the government has exempted income distributed through discretionary testamentary trusts from a proposed 30 per cent minimum tax rate, a policy critics branded as a death tax by stealth. The government also removed nine separate discretionary powers originally granted to the treasurer, which would have allowed ministerial control over housing definitions and asset discounts.

Despite the scale of the concessions, neither the Coalition nor major industry bodies see them as a complete fix to what they say is a toxic budget. Angus Taylor has declared the budget is "in tatters" and demanded the scrapping of the entire bill, not just piecemeal carve-outs.

Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox argued that the amendments lessened but did not eliminate the broader economic harm. Mr Willox pointed out that the core legislation still raised taxes to punitive levels for medium and large enterprises, applied rates retrospectively, and penalised investment and innovation.

Because official consultations on various tranches of the tax package remained open, the frantic policy rewrite resembled a firefighting exercise rather than an orderly legislative process. The hasty adjustments indicate further amendments are likely as the government quietly finalises decisions behind closed doors.

Labor has paid a heavy price for what voters viewed as blatant electoral overreach. The bruising retreat does not erase the political stigma stemming from the Prime Minister's pre-election assurances that a Labor government would not alter negative gearing or capital gains tax frameworks.

Hanson's "fire the liar" campaign has achieved significant cut-through since the budget, reportedly raising millions of dollars for her One Nation party.

By overestimating its mandate and attempting what many people see as an ideologically driven tax hike on the back of a lie, Labor misjudged the electorate, suffered a severe political blow and has handed its opponents an effective weapon ahead of the next election.
